titleStmt.title: No. 931
The Ambassador in Egypt (Caffery) to the Department of State

div.head:
No. 931
The Ambassador in Egypt (Caffery) to the Department of State
div.p: The following comments are in response to the five points set forth at the end of the Department’s instruction under reference.

1. The elements of a final settlement between the country of assignment and Israel, irrespective of assessments of the possibility of moving at this time. A detailed statement is desired referring where appropriate to the specific objectives set forth above.
Egypt is far less concerned over the Palestine question than any of the other Arab States. GOE objectives for a final settlement would probably boil down to the following points:

list.item: a. A land connection between Egypt and Jordan. Present GOE thinking on this point seems to involve the cession by Israel of a strip cutting across the southern and eastern Negev from Aqaba to the Mediterranean eliminating any Israeli port on the Gulf of Aqaba. (The Egyptians seem to feel that Jordan would not be interested in port facilities at Haifa if the Gaza corridor were achieved.)
b. Disposal of the Gaza Strip and its refugees.
c. In general any settlement would have to have minimum acceptability to the other Arab States.

div.p: 2. The pros and cons of attempting an across-the-board settlement supplementing the present step-by-step approach.

Egypt would probably go along with an across-the-board settlement acceptable to the other Arab States but would not attempt one in the face of their opposition. It is believed that even the suggestion of an across-the-board settlement at this time would frighten the GOE and probably diminish their enthusiasm for the step-by-step approach. At the moment they are fully occupied in eliminating the Moslem Brotherhood and will be very timid for a time even about new moves in the step-by-step approach.
3. General views on tactics including particularly the appropriateness of the Trieste technique.
The Trieste technique would seem to be the most hopeful way of attacking the situation. In considering this technique, however, the following thoughts may open up a useful supplementary tactic.

The Palestine refugees are a key group which must be taken into consideration in seeking a settlement. Not only is it true that their assent is essential, but it is equally true that the Arab Governments would have the utmost difficulty in negotiating and agreeing to as reasonable a settlement as the refugees themselves could accept. Consequently it is suggested that a hand picked and cooperative “Palestine Goverment” might be created to replace the shadowy and dubious existing “Government.” Such a Palestine Government could negotiate on behalf of the Palestinians and would be able to make bolder and more realistic decisions than could the Arab Governments. Moreover, the latter probably could not, or at least would not feel obliged to sound off publicly with intransigent tirades in the name of the refugees against any settlement such a Government might agree to.

There are a considerable number of Palestinian refugees who accept the fact of the existence of Israel and who believe that it would be possible to select and set up such a Palestinian Government if the US and the UK were prepared to give them strong support. This would help meet the refugees’ need for social cohesion. Such a move, in addition to the benefits already indicated, would also have the advantage of neutralizing to some extent those individuals
such as the ex-Grand Mufti of Jerusalem who seek to sabotage every constructive move. Finally, it would help to diminish the feelings of hostility and distrust directed against the present Arab Governments by so many of the refugees.

list.item: a. Would approaches to individual Arab countries singly be preferable to simultaneous approaches to two or more of the Arab countries?

The possibilities inherent in the above suggestion could be explored in Egypt first. If the idea appears promising these preliminaries will open the way to further exploration, particularly in Jordan. In any event, approaches to individual Arab countries singly would appear to open better prospects than simultaneous approaches.
b. Under optimum conditions what timing would appear reasonable?

Assuming that the first approach would be made to Egypt as the most receptive country, the timing should be gauged in the light of the GOE’s internal situation (particularly vis-à-vis the Moslem Brotherhood) and the state of its current relations with the other Arab States. The latter is important if absolute secrecy can not be maintained.
c. What would be the reaction if the initial approach is made through Egypt?

div.p: Other considerations aside, the GOE would probably accept being chosen for the initial approach.

4. What inducements from the US, UK or other outside countries would be most effective in the country of assignment? If economic or military aid is recommended, general estimates of the magnitude and duration would be helpful.

In the case of Egypt economic and military aid are recommended as inducements. A major problem is to help Egypt overcome its inferiority complex vis-á-vis Israel, particularly in the sphere of military defense. This would probably require two or three years of carefully selected military aid.
5. The usefulness of endeavoring to move forward simultaneously on area defense arrangements.

Efforts to move forward on area defense arrangements should be continued since there is hope that Egypt will come along in time and quite possible start a rush to get on the band-wagon. By giving the Arab States a sense of participation, and consequently of importance, their intransigent attitude towards Israel may be partially sublimated as their feelings of frustration diminish.
